items.originalTitle: 2028 Democrats say Nvidia news is another example of corruption in government
items.author: Jason Beeferman and Sam Sutton
items.title: 2028 Democrats say Nvidia news is another example of corruption in government
items.summary: Democrats weighing 2028 presidential bids are using Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as another opportunity to accuse the White House of corruption. It’s a message that appeared to work well for them earlier this month: Voters resoundingly rejected President Donald Trump’s agenda, angry over high prices and an economy that benefited a select few. Now, Democrats are keen to repeat that core political argument — especially after Trump took credit for helping reinstate Huang. “This is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said in a statement . “The sheer corruption and weakness of Donald Trump is hurting America and putting our economy and national security at risk,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro wrote in a statement , describing Huang’s reinstatement is an example of “a rigged system that protects those at the very top.” Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel told Decoded by POLITICO: “The number one rule is that the rule of law will hold the banker, the billionaire, and the baker to the same standard,” he said. “Now you tell me: What’s good about capitalism when you have a president of the United States pressing a public board to reverse themselves on their own governance? What is good about that decision?” Pritzker, Shapiro and Emanuel are among the wide field of prospective Democratic presidential candidates. Their immediate decision to criticize Huang’s return as head of the massive chip company puts them at odds with top Silicon Valley leaders , including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to be reinstated after he stepped down. The public statements also show that these top Democrats are holding onto the playbook that campaigns used to dominate in the midterm elections, when the party firmly regained control of the House, Senate and statehouses around the country. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and two company employees . On Monday, he was reinstated by a unanimous board vote after Trump publicly called for his return and pushed for it with board members over the weekend. Huang’s close relationship with Trump has come under scrutiny since news of his affairs broke. The two spoke frequently, with Trump even calling Huang directly while he was on stage at a tech conference. The New York Times previously reported that Trump and top administration officials were aware that Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy — but chose not to act. And Trump critics from both parties have pointed to Nvidia’s $25 million donation to the president’s White House ballroom project under Huang’s leadership as an example of Trump’s alleged corruption. In a statement, the White House said that “today’s decision by Nvidia will preserve America’s technological edge over China, strengthen our national security, and ensure the future of SI continues to be built in America.” “The Huang situation at its core is about corruption,” Republican former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who is considering another presidential bid , said last week, referencing the ballroom donation. “So when something came up that was serious, what happened? Trump walked away from it and wouldn’t deal with it. That’s the intersection of corruption and incompetence that causes the American people to lose.” Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who also is considering a bid, told Axios the move from Huang amounted to a double standard for Trump’s allies and the rest of America. "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee,” he said. “You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate where, frankly, if that was any of us we would be held to a different type of standard.” That messaging could continue to prove effective. During the midterms, Democratic groups zeroed in on corruption in the White House and sought to connect high gas and grocery prices to a Trump administration they said flouted basic ethical rules while protecting and enriching powerful allies of the president. They connected corruption to the Epstein files, data centers , stock trading and other topics, reinforcing that unscrupulous dealings were at play while costs were going up. Polling obtained by POLITICO in the weeks leading up to Election Day shows the vast majority of Americans — both Democrats and Republicans — say corruption is driving up their costs. And a September poll from Gallup also found about 90 percent of Americans believe corruption is rampant in government. Democrats and several Republicans on Capitol Hill are pushing for more transparency on the extent to which Nvidia’s chips ended up in Chinese hands and further details on Huang’s relationship with suspected spy Alice Huang. “Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy,” Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is running to lead Senate Democrats, said in a briefing to reporters. Van Hollen was speculated as a possible 2028 presidential candidate, though he’s now ruled out a White House bid. “We know that President Trump owns Nvidia stock. We know that Jensen Huang contributed to the inauguration, attended a million-dollar plate at Mar-a-Lago and essentially Jensen Huang has been running the Trump administration's AI and big tech policy,” Van Hollen added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Russia Accuses Estonia of Hostilities ‘On the Verge of Triggering Open War’
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
items.title: Russia Accuses Estonia of Hostilities ‘On the Verge of Triggering Open War’
items.summary: —Getty Images Russia has accused Estonia of bringing the two countries to the brink of “open war.” The Russian foreign ministry on Monday lodged a formal protest with the Estonian charge d’affaires in Moscow over Estonia’s decision to close its road border crossings with Russia. The ministry said the border closure was among several other “hostile” and “Russophobic” moves taken against Russia in recent years, adding that Russia reserves the right to respond with measures to protect its national interests. “The Estonian diplomat was once again told that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering ​open war with Russia,” the ministry said in a statement laying out the accusations. “Tallinn apparently isn’t seriously considering the consequences of such a move,” the ministry warned. Tensions between the Eastern European neighbors have sharply escalated since Estonia announced on Friday plans to close all road crossings with Russia for at least six months from December 1. Estonia’s decision came after it accused Russian intelligence of a foiled arson plot at an Estonian drone factory, which Moscow denied. Estonian Charge d'Affaires Marek Uhtegi leaves the Russian Foreign Ministry headquarters in Moscow after being summoned over Estonia's closure of its shared border with Russia on Nov. 23, 2026. —Kirill Zykov—Sputnik/AP Estonia’s foreign minister Margus ​Tsahkna dismissed Russia’s claims and said Moscow is responsible for “the real security threats” in Europe. “Russia is flooding ⁠the airwaves with baseless accusations against Estonia to distract from its own actions undermining European security,” Tsahkna posted on X on Monday. As a member of both the NATO alliance and the European Union, Estonia would be entitled to assistance from members of both blocs if Russia launched an attack on Estonian territory. Asked about Russia’s accusations on Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said NATO was monitoring the security situation in Estonia and that the alliance had options to respond if needed. Here’s what to know about the recent hostilities between Russia and Estonia. What is Russia accusing Estonia of? Russia’s foreign ministry said Estonia’s decision to close their road border is the latest of “numerous hostile actions” taken against Russia. It accused the Estonian government of “tacitly” allowing Ukraine to use its airspace to attack Russia. Russia has previously accused Estonia and other NATO Baltic states of letting Ukrainian drones use their airspace. Since Russia invaded the country in February 2022, Ukrainian drones have entered NATO airspace on multiple occasions, although NATO countries have denied permitting drones to use their airspace. The Ukrainian government said the incursions were a result of diversions caused by Russian electronic warfare. Estonia rejected the allegation in a statement on Monday. “While we generally do not comment on or engage with Russian propaganda narratives, in this case we can reiterate that Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country,” Estonia’s foreign ministry told Reuters . The Russian foreign ministry also accused Estonia of attempting to obstruct the movement of Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, including trying to “inspect, seize, and detain them with the aim of imposing a naval blockade” on Russia. Estonia’s navy boarded and detained a Russia-bound tanker in April 2025, saying it lacked a valid flag, and attempted to stop another Russia-bound tanker the following month. There is no official blockade, and a senior Estonian commander told Reuters in April that the navy would refrain from detaining Russia’s shadow fleet vessels because of the risk of a military confrontation. Russia’s foreign ministry pointed to Estonia’s Oct. 8 ban on the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through its territory as another example of a “hostile” action against Russia. The E.U. tariffs grain imports from Russia and Belarus, citing Russia’s seizure of Ukrainian grain, although it allows shipments to transit the E.U. Estonia’s foreign ministry said Russia was looking for alternatives to Black Sea export routes and that Estonia would preventively keep its ports from serving as an outlet for Russian grain and potential revenue to fund the war. Russia’s foreign ministry also alleged that the Estonian government imposed oppressive measures on Russian-speaking residents in Estonia. Among the alleged actions are a ban on the Russian language “at all levels,” criminal prosecutions and deportations of Russia sympathizers, and the threat of dissolving a Russian orthodox church in Estonia. Estonia did not respond to those allegations in its statement. There is no official ban on the Russian language in Estonia. The government mandates Estonian in official settings and is phasing out Russian as a main teaching language in some kindergartens and schools as part of a transition to Estonian-language instruction . Russian is the mother tongue of around 27% of Estonia’s population , according to government data. The Estonian Christian Orthodox Church and Pühtitsa Convent face a Dec. 28 deadline to comply with a law restricting ties to foreign religious bodies deemed a security threat, or face dissolution. Estonian law restricts administrative ties to Moscow, although it allows religious ties. The church has challenged the law at the European Court of Human Rights. Why have Russian and Estonian relations broken down? Relations between Russia and Estonia have been strained for years, and they further deteriorated after Russia invaded Ukraine. Although Soviet Russia recognized Estonia as an independent state in 1920, Moscow has long sought to exert influence over its neighbor. The Soviet Union annexed Estonia in 1940 during World War II, before Nazi Germany occupied the Baltic state from 1941 to 1944. Soviet forces retook Estonia and placed it under Moscow’s rule until 1991, when Estonia regained its independence. The same year, the two countries restored diplomatic relations, and Russia began a phased withdrawal of its troops. In 2004, Estonia joined both NATO and the E.U. Its border with Russia thus became part of the E.U.’s external border. A decade later, Estonia and Russia signed treaties defining their land border and maritime boundaries, but the treaties were never ratified. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine triggered a breakdown in diplomatic ties. Estonia closed Russia’s consular offices in Narva and Tartu in 2022. In January 2023, the two countries expelled their ambassadors and downgraded bilateral representation to charges d’affaires. Tensions have continued to escalate as the war has dragged on. In September 2025, NATO said three Russian fighter jets entered Estonian airspace. Earlier this year, Estonia began introducing overnight closures at certain road checkpoints, citing border incidents from the Russian side. Where could things go from here? In recent weeks, Russia has escalated pressure on other countries bordering Ukraine. Last week, two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed on Poland during a major Russian attack on Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared to be a deliberate provocation coinciding with European military drills in Poland. Days earlier, Moldova detected seven drones in its airspace amid Russian strikes on Ukraine, prompting it to summon Moscow’s ambassador-designate. Estonian authorities said Russia’s military intelligence agency ordered an attempted arson on Estonian drone maker Threod Systems on Nov. 14. Moscow denied involvement. “We do not warn about these threats without reason,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said about the foiled attack. Margo Palloson, Estonia’s domestic intelligence chief, told public broadcaster ERR that Russia has targeted around 10 Estonian defense companies. In a Politico op-ed published Tuesday, Tsahkna said Estonia was closing its land border in response to “a growing number of acts of sabotage and intimidation” by Russia. He cited Polish authorities’ allegations that Russian intelligence services were behind an arson attack on Warsaw’s Marywilska shopping center, Germany’s discovery of an alleged Russian explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport, and Denmark’s claim that it foiled an alleged Russian intelligence plot to kill an American-Ukrainian citizen. “These incidents form part of a broader Russian campaign targeting the whole of Europe, including countries far beyond its borders. The aim is to undermine the European security order, intimidate its neighbors and dictate the choices of sovereign nations,” Tsahkna wrote. “Closing our border will not eliminate these threats, but it will limit opportunities for hostile intelligence activities. It will also help close channels for sanctions evasion, a crucial part of depriving Russia of the resources it uses to finance its war economy and sustain its aggression.” Whether the latest dispute will lead to open conflict is uncertain. Jennifer Kavanagh and Jeremy Shapiro argued in a December 2025 European Council on Foreign Relations report that a limited, deniable operation designed to test NATO’s unity was more likely than a direct Russian invasion of Estonia. An armed attack by Russia on Estonia could trigger NATO’s collective defense obligations, raising the risk of a wider war in Europe. Rutte reassured in October that there was “no imminent threat against NATO territory.” Leonard Schütte, an expert on transatlantic security, wrote in May for the German Marshall Fund , however, that doubts about U.S. commitment to Europe could make Moscow more willing to test NATO in the next few years. In September, Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem said Russia could be in a position to use military force against Estonia within a year if fighting in Ukraine ended within six months. “Russia could use a military force of size ‘X’ against us. Are our preparations matching that? Are we capable of eliminating a military force of that size? And if we are not, then we should make those necessary preparations?” Herem said. “Or there is another option: We can all sign off on keeping our fingers crossed that it will not happen and do nothing at all.”

There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment. Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond girl.

items.originalTitle: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?

items.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
items.summary: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

items.originalTitle: Hakeem Jeffries Can Live With “Medicare for More”
items.author: Jessica Washington
items.title: Hakeem Jeffries Can Live With “Medicare for More”
items.summary: After years of being able to hide behind Republicans’ blatant mismanagement and intentional sabotage of the healthcare system, Democrats will now have to put forth their own plan to save our crumbling healthcare infrastructure. Whether the party can agree on what that plan is remains to be seen. The middle path has been dubbed “Medicare for More.” It’s been framed variously as a first step toward Medicare for All and as a half-measure to relieve the pressure to pass the more expansive healthcare agenda. Now backed by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the presumed next speaker of the House, the policy would lower the eligibility age for the public retiree health system; expand dental, vision, and hearing care; and provide universal coverage for children. “We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare.” But the plan would maintain the status quo for people ages 26 to 55 — many of whom saw their Affordable Care Act healthcare premiums spike after December 2025, when enhanced subsidies expired for an estimated 22 million people as a result of Republicans ’ so-called Big, Beautiful Bill. “We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare,” Rep. Summer Lee, D-Penn., wrote in a statement to the Intercept. “The mandate from voters is change. The American people literally cannot afford to return to the status quo.” Progressives have vowed to pass Medicare for All, a sweeping proposal to establish a national public health insurance program sponsored by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. Backers of the full Medicare for All package argue that systemwide change is necessary — and that half-measures are not what voters asked the party to do. Polling suggests broad support for Medicare for All, particularly among Democratic voters. A Kaiser Family Foundation poll found that 94 percent of registered Democrats support the policy — and roughly 79 percent of all adults polled favor the federal government doing more to help provide health insurance. Despite Medicare for All’s growing popularity, Jeffries, a New York Democrat, remained skeptical of the policy throughout the midterms. In August, he told “Meet the Press” that he did not support it, emphasizing that since joining leadership he has declined to co-sponsor Medicare for All legislation. Related Luigi, a Year Later: How to Build a Movement Against Parasitic Health Insurance Giants Jayapal, who has reintroduced her signature legislation every session since 2019 and plans to do so again in the next Congress, said wins from candidates who ran on Medicare for All in this year’s midterm elections have helped to push leadership on this issue. She specifically cited the success of purple-state candidates like Sen.-elects Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, who invoked the policy again and again on the campaign trail — and won. At a meeting of the Congressional Progressive Caucus last week, the Washington congresswoman said that Jeffries agreed to two out of three of the caucus’s requests on Medicare for All. First, he agreed to support the initial phase-in of the Medicare for All Act, which Jayapal says she has been pushing him on for “the last couple of months.” The plan would greatly expand access to healthcare for most Americans by simultaneously lowering the Medicare eligibility age and covering everyone under the age of 18. Second, he agreed to get a Congressional Budget Office score on the full Medicare for All act. The CBO score estimates the cost of any given legislation, which gives members a chance to weigh the financial impact of a bill before casting their vote. But Jeffries declined to support their third request: a markup of the full “Medicare for All” bill in committee. Markups allow committees to make amendments to a bill before it gets voted on in front of the full House — making it substantially easier to pass. Still, Jayapal believes there is a path forward for her bill. She said that she has spoken with both new members and incumbents “who haven’t been on it before” and now say they want to co-sponsor the bill, and she believes that with more of the caucus’s support, Jeffries could support a bill markup in the future. It appears that attacks on the policy have become less effective with voters over time. Private insurance companies have long supported anti-Medicare for All messaging, Jayapal pointed out. Opponents of the public healthcare proposal argue it will create longer wait times, raise taxes, and separate people from their preferred doctors. But as the state of healthcare in the United States has degraded and become more dystopian, Jayapal said, “none of those attacks work when people are already experiencing $20,000 in premiums, when they’re already being told they can’t have care by an AI model or by a private insurance company.” Related Corporations Are The Real Healthcare Fraudsters, Inspector General Report Shows Regardless of what the public wants, and even if Democrats can agree on a vision, the mercurial commander-in-chief remains an obstacle. The Democrats’ 56-seat Senate majority is significant but not veto-proof, and President Donald Trump has previously called Medicare for All a “socialist takeover.” On Saturday, he told Fox News there’s a “chance” he would work with Democrats on healthcare — but it would not be the legislation Democrats “want.” Jayapal says she’s not holding out much hope for collaboration. “I don’t think much about Trump in this particular moment,” she said. “I think we just need to do the thing that we know Americans deserve and want, and then let’s send it to his desk. And if he signs it, great. And if he doesn’t, he will be the one that is not allowing Americans to have healthcare, and then we can sign it when we have the trifecta.” The post Hakeem Jeffries Can Live With “Medicare for More” appeared first on The Intercept .
